questions.title: How exactly does BOFT(m, b) reduce to OFT as special cases?
questions.question_body: The paper claims BOFT(1, b) reduces to block-diagonal OFT with block size b, and BOFT(1, d) reduces to the original OFT with a full orthogonal. Could someone write out the explicit form of R(m, b) for m=1 and show how it matches diag(R_1, ..., R_{d/b}) for block-diagonal OFT, and how setting b=d gives a single dense orthogonal factor?

questions.title: Deriving the parameter count: why is BOFT(m, b) said to use (1/2)(b-1) d m trainable parameters?
questions.question_body: I am trying to reconcile the claimed parameter count with the construction. Each BOFT component is said to decompose into blocks of size $2b \times 2b$ (or $2 \times 2$ when $b=2$) that are parameterized via Cayley transforms. How do we count the independent degrees of freedom per block under orthogonality and then sum across the $d$-dimensional layer and $m$ components to arrive at $\tfrac{1}{2}(b-1) d m$?

questions.title: How does the Cayley transform guarantee orthogonality for each butterfly component?
questions.question_body: The paper uses the Cayley parameterization $R=(I+Q)(I-Q)^{-1}$ with $Q=-Q^\top$ for orthogonality. For a butterfly component $\tilde{B}^b(d, k)$, which is a block-structured sparse matrix, are we applying the Cayley transform to each $2b \times 2b$ block independently? If so, could someone show that this blockwise Cayley construction implies $\tilde{B}^b(d, k)^\top \tilde{B}^b(d, k) = I$ for the whole component, especially when blocks are permuted?

questions.title: Handling non-power-of-two dimensions: what happens when d is not a power of 2?
questions.question_body: The butterfly definition assumes $d = 2^N$. In practice many layer widths are not powers of 2. Do we pad dimensions, mix sizes via ragged blocks, or use generalized butterfly factors for non-power-of-two $d$? How does this affect parameter count and the guarantee of dense connectivity after composing $m$ factors?

questions.title: Does BOFT produce a dense orthogonal matrix for arbitrary m and b?
questions.question_body: The paper states that BOFT($\log \tfrac{2d}{b}$, $b$) yields a dense orthogonal matrix. Is there a formal condition relating $m$, $b$, and $d$ under which the product $R(m, b) = \prod_{i=1}^m \tilde{B}^b_{(d,i)}$ is guaranteed to be dense? What goes wrong (in terms of the induced graph connectivity) if $m$ is smaller than $\log \tfrac{2d}{b}$?

questions.title: Information transmission view: how do edges correspond to trainable parameters exactly?
questions.question_body: In the grid graph analogy, edges reflect nonzeros that allow information flow. The text distinguishes 'necessary' edges (to ensure full rank and orthogonality) from 'free' edges (trainable). Could someone formalize: given an orthogonal factor $B_i$, which nonzero entries are determined up to signs or coupling by orthogonality, and which correspond to independent parameters? How does this mapping justify comparing total edge counts to parameter counts?

questions.title: Why is the minimum number of edges between adjacent levels at least d under orthogonality?
questions.question_body: The paper says each $B_i$ must be full rank, which requires $d$ edges forming a bijection between level $i$ and level $i+1$. Could someone give a linear-algebraic argument that an orthogonal matrix must have at least $d$ structurally independent nonzeros (e.g., a permutation structure), and clarify how this relates to the 'necessary' edges being non-trainable or constrained to $\pm 1$?

questions.title: Expressivity: can BOFT approximate any orthogonal with fewer than O(d^2) parameters?
questions.question_body: Theorem 1 suggests that multiplying a sequence of butterfly matrices and their transposes in a kaleidoscope hierarchy can represent the entire orthogonal group when $l=d-1$, $m_1=m_2=\log d$, and $b_1=b_2=2$. Does this imply an exact parameterization of $O(d)$ with $O(d \log d \cdot d)$ parameters (thus still superlinear)? Is there any bound that shows approximation of a generic orthogonal matrix within $\varepsilon$ using only $O(d \log d)$ parameters?

questions.title: What exactly makes BOFT more expressive than block-diagonal OFT for the same block size?
questions.question_body: The paper states BOFT is 'provably more expressive' than OFT with the same $b$. Is there a formal inclusion result like $\mathcal{F}_{\text{OFT}, b} \subsetneq \mathcal{F}_{\text{BOFT}, b}$, and can you provide a constructive example of a matrix in BOFT($m, b$) that cannot be represented by block-diagonal OFT($1, b$)?

questions.title: What is the computational cost of applying BOFT during training and at inference?
questions.question_body: For a linear layer $W^0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times n}$, BOFT applies left-multiplication by $R(m, b)$. What is the forward-time complexity in terms of $d$, $n$, $m$, and $b$ if we exploit the sparse structure of each butterfly component? Also, once training is done and we fold $R$ into $W^0$, is the inference-time cost identical to a standard dense matrix multiply with the same $W$?

questions.title: Why does orthogonal finetuning preserve the spectral norm of the weight matrix?
questions.question_body: The paper claims that for $W^0 = U \Sigma V^\top$ and finetuned weights $RW^0 = (RU)\Sigma V^\top$, the spectral norm is preserved. I follow that left multiplication by an orthogonal matrix does not change singular values, but is this still true if $R$ is an approximate orthogonal due to numerical issues in the Cayley inversion $(I-Q)^{-1}$? Are there practical stabilization steps to ensure this property holds during training?

questions.title: How is multiplicative Dropout implemented without breaking orthogonality?
questions.question_body: The paper proposes selecting some percentage of butterfly components and $2b \times 2b$ blocks within them and replacing those blocks with identity matrices during training. Does this preserve overall orthogonality of the product $R$ at each step? Is the masking resampled every iteration like standard Dropout, and does it bias the expected transform (e.g., is $\mathbb{E}[R]$ equal to the un-dropped $R$)?

questions.title: Initialization: does setting all Q=0 in the Cayley transform ensure identity for the entire BOFT product?
questions.question_body: Each block uses $R=(I+Q)(I-Q)^{-1}$ with $Q=0$ giving the identity. If every block within each butterfly component is initialized to identity, then $R(m, b)$ is the identity. Is there any subtle interaction due to the fixed permutations between components that could make the product deviate from identity at initialization?

questions.title: Stability of the Cayley transform: is (I - Q) always invertible for skew-symmetric Q?
questions.question_body: Since $Q$ is skew-symmetric, its eigenvalues are purely imaginary. Then $(I - Q)$ has no zero eigenvalues, so it should be invertible. Are there numerical conditioning issues for large $\|Q\|$? Do you clip or reparameterize $Q$ (e.g., via a scaled skew-symmetric) to maintain stable inverses during training?

questions.title: How are the permutations between butterfly components chosen and are they learnable?
questions.question_body: The construction refers to each $\tilde{B}(d, k)$ as a 'blockwise permutation' of $\tilde{B}(d, 2)$. Are these permutations fixed a priori by a standard butterfly schedule (like Cooley-Tukey radix-2), or is there any learnable choice over the permutation pattern? If fixed, could learnable permutations improve expressivity at the same parameter count?

questions.title: Clarifying the notation: what does BOFT(m, b) mean when the text defines R(m, b) using b/2?
questions.question_body: The paper writes: 'For convenience, we denote BOFT with $R(m, \tfrac{b}{2})$ as BOFT($m, b$)'. This confuses me. Does 'b' in BOFT($m, b$) denote the $2b \times 2b$ block size, or the block dimension used in the block-diagonal baseline? Could someone restate the exact shapes of the elementary blocks and how that maps to the $b$ reported in experiments?

questions.title: What is the exact condition under which BOFT achieves dense connectivity in the grid graph?
questions.question_body: In the information-transmission picture, dense connectivity means every source node reaches every sink node. For the butterfly sequence $\tilde{B}(d, d), \tilde{B}(d, d/2), \dots, \tilde{B}(d, 2)$, can someone provide a proof sketch that this sequence realizes all pairwise connections across levels, and therefore the product matrix is dense (ignoring measure-zero parameter settings that could introduce accidental zeros)?

questions.title: BOFT vs. Householder/CSR/Rotation factorizations for orthogonals: trade-offs?
questions.question_body: One can parameterize any orthogonal as a product of $O(d)$ Householder reflections or Givens rotations, which leads to $O(d^2)$ parameters if we make them dense. How does BOFT compare in terms of parameter count, computational cost, and approximation quality to such classical factorizations when used for finetuning? Is there a principled reason BOFT's structured sparsity should regularize better than, say, a learned sequence of Givens rotations?

questions.title: How does BOFT differ from reparameterizing W directly with a butterfly parameterization (e.g., Monarch)?
questions.question_body: The related work contrasts BOFT's left-multiplicative, layer-shared orthogonal transform $R$ with approaches that parameterize $W$ directly as a butterfly-structured matrix. Could someone explain the representational difference: does $RW^0$ preserve pairwise neuron angles by construction, while a butterfly $W$ does not? Are there scenarios where directly parameterizing $W$ would be strictly more expressive for finetuning than composing with $R$?

questions.title: Application details: to which weight matrices is BOFT applied in transformers?
questions.question_body: For LLMs and vision transformers, do you apply $R$ to all linear layers (attention $Q/K/V/O$, MLP projections), or only a subset? If applied to, say, $W_Q \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$ per attention head, is $R$ shared across heads or per-head? How do you handle layers where $d \neq n$ (rectangular $W^0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times n}$)?

questions.title: Does BOFT preserve pairwise neuron angles exactly, like OFT, when m>1?
questions.question_body: OFT preserves pairwise angles between neurons because all columns are transformed by the same orthogonal matrix. BOFT applies a product of orthogonals $R(m, b)$ shared across columns, so it should also be orthogonal. Can someone confirm that for any $m$, as long as $R(m, b)$ is orthogonal, the pairwise angles of columns in $W^0$ are exactly preserved?

questions.title: Training dynamics: does the non-commutativity of orthogonal factors matter for optimization?
questions.question_body: Since $\tilde{B}^b_{(d,i)} \tilde{B}^b_{(d,j)} \neq \tilde{B}^b_{(d,j)} \tilde{B}^b_{(d,i)}$ in general, the order of components matters. Is the order fixed as in the canonical butterfly schedule? Have you observed sensitivity to permuting the order of the components, and could reordering during training help escape bad minima?

questions.title: Interpreting the 'weight interpolation' property in BOFT
questions.question_body: The paper mentions an 'intriguing weight interpolation' due to factorization (Figure referenced). What exactly is being interpolated? Is it that intermediate products $R_t = \prod_{i=1}^t \tilde{B}_i$ provide a path on the orthogonal manifold from identity to the final $R$, akin to a homotopy? Does this have practical benefits such as smoother training or better early stopping?

questions.title: How does Multiplicative Dropout interact with gradients through the Cayley transform?
questions.question_body: When blocks are replaced with identity during dropout, their parameters are effectively masked. Do you stop gradients for those blocks for that step, or do you use a straight-through estimator? Also, does dropout-before-Cayley vs dropout-after-Cayley make a difference for maintaining orthogonality and gradient stability?

questions.title: Can BOFT be composed with LoRA, and if so, in what order?
questions.question_body: Since LoRA is additive $W = W^0 + BA$, and BOFT is multiplicative $W = RW^0$, is there a sensible combined parameterization, e.g., $W = R(W^0 + BA)$ or $W = RW^0 + BA$? Would this interfere with the spectral-norm preservation and angle-preservation properties that motivate BOFT?

questions.title: Does the butterfly inductive bias risk hurting tasks that need highly localized adaptations?
questions.question_body: The paper argues butterfly structure provides a helpful inductive bias because it can express many classic transforms. But if a downstream task requires very localized changes (akin to a small subset of coordinates), could the global mixing enforced by butterfly cause over-smoothing? Is there empirical evidence on tasks where block-diagonal OFT outperforms BOFT due to locality?

questions.title: How does BOFT handle convolutional layers or weight tensors not easily flattened to d x n?
questions.question_body: In CNNs or diffusion U-Nets, many weights are 4D tensors. Is BOFT applied after reshaping kernels to $d \times n$ matrices, and if so, along which dimension is the orthogonal $R$ applied? Does this reshaping choice affect the inductive bias or performance?

questions.title: Why does the paper say block-diagonal OFT 'cannot approximate classic linear transforms'?
questions.question_body: It is stated that block-diagonal orthogonals reduce expressiveness and cannot approximate classic transforms like DFT. Is there a formal argument that a block-diagonal orthogonal with block size $b \ll d$ cannot approximate a dense transform such as DFT in operator norm unless $b$ scales with $d$?

questions.title: What is meant by 'minimum free edges' in the information transmission criteria?
questions.question_body: The desiderata include 'dense connectivity' and 'minimum free edges'. Could someone formalize the optimization problem implied here? Is there a precise graph-theoretic measure of free edges tied to the number of independent parameters under orthogonality constraints, and is the butterfly topology known to be near-optimal for this measure?
